responses.sql: SELECT staff_id, SUM(amount) AS total_amount, SUM(amount) / SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () AS fraction_of_total FROM payment WHERE rental_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY staff_id

assumptions.assumption: Payments that link to a rental means payment.rental_id IS NOT NULL. The fraction's denominator is the total across only those linked payments, not all payments.
The staff member is the one recorded on the payment (payment.staff_id), not the one on the related rental.

responses.sql: SELECT staff_id, SUM(amount) AS total_amount, SUM(amount) / SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () AS fraction_of_total FROM payment WHERE rental_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY staff_id

assumptions.assumption: "Payments that link to a rental" means payment.rental_id IS NOT NULL. The combined total across all staff is taken over those same filtered payments, so the fractions sum to 1.
Staff are identified by payment.staff_id, the staff member who took the payment. rental.staff_id is a different thing and is not used.

responses.sql: SELECT staff_id, SUM(amount) AS total_amount, SUM(amount) * 1.0 / SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () AS fraction_of_total FROM payment WHERE rental_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY staff_id ORDER BY staff_id

assumptions.assumption: Payments that link to a rental means payment.rental_id IS NOT NULL. I did not join to the rental table, so a non-null rental_id that points to no rental row would still count.
The staff member is the one who recorded the payment (payment.staff_id), not the one who handled the rental (rental.staff_id). Both are grouping columns with the same two values.
The combined total in the denominator covers only the payments that link to a rental, so the fractions sum to 1.

alternatives.interpretation: Attribute each payment to the staff member on the linked rental (rental.staff_id) instead of the staff member who recorded the payment. This also requires the rental row to exist.
